title: Your Gut Bacteria Decide How Many Calories You Actually Absorb. A New Model Just Proved It.
excerpt: Arizona State researchers built a mathematical model that tracks food beyond the label. For South Asians losing their traditional diet, the implications are enormous.
body:
For more than a century, the calorie counts on food labels have relied on a system invented in the 1890s by Wilbur Atwater. Multiply protein, carbohydrate and fat content by their average energy values, and you get a number. That number has guided dietary advice, obesity interventions and insurance tables for generations.

It has also been wrong — or at least incomplete. A new mathematical model developed at Arizona State University has quantified exactly how wrong, and the answer matters far more for South Asians than for most other populations on Earth.

The model, called DAMM (Digestion, Absorption, and Microbial Metabolism), was published in PLOS ONE in May 2026. It does what Atwater factors never could: it tracks food all the way through the digestive system, including the trillions of microbes in the colon that transform leftover material into compounds the body can absorb.

The results upend a basic assumption. Participants eating a Western diet — processed food, smaller particle sizes, less fibre — absorbed roughly 116 more calories per day than those eating a high-fibre, microbiome-enhancing diet. The two groups ate meals with identical calorie labels. The difference came entirely from what happened inside the gut.

The Microbial Middlemen

DAMM splits digestion into two zones. About 85 per cent of usable energy is absorbed in the upper gastrointestinal tract, where the body does most of the familiar work of breaking down food. The remaining 15 per cent comes from the lower tract — the colon — where gut bacteria ferment whatever escaped earlier digestion.

Those bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which the body absorbs as an additional energy source. On average, DAMM estimated that SCFAs contributed about 140 calories per day, or roughly 7.4 per cent of total usable energy. On the high-fibre diet, the microbes received more fermentable material and produced more SCFAs. On the Western diet, less material reached the colon, but the body absorbed more calories upstream.

The net effect: the Western diet delivers a hidden calorie surplus that no food label captures.

"Digestion is not just a human process — it is a collaboration between our bodies and trillions of microbes living in the gut," said Professor Rosa Krajmalnik-Brown, who directs the Biodesign Center for Health Through Microbiomes at ASU. "DAMM gives us a powerful new way to quantify how those microbial partners contribute to human health and energy balance."

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The DAMM findings land on a body of evidence that should alarm every Indian who has traded dal-chawal for drive-through meals.

A landmark study published in npj Biofilms and Microbiomes tracked the gut microbiomes of Indians living in India, recent Indian immigrants to Canada, and Indo-Canadians born abroad. The findings were stark. Indians in India harboured abundant Prevotella copri, a bacterium that thrives on the complex carbohydrates found in lentils, whole grains, and vegetables. That bacterium declined sharply in immigrants and was even lower in the second generation.

The loss is not cosmetic. Prevotella copri helps break down plant fibre into those same short-chain fatty acids that DAMM shows are central to healthy energy balance. Losing it means less efficient fibre fermentation, fewer SCFAs, and a gut environment that increasingly resembles the Western profile — one that, according to DAMM, absorbs more calories from the same food.

For first-generation NRIs, the transition is dietary. For their children, it may be generational. The Canadian study found that Indo-Canadians who had never lived in India had gut microbiomes that looked more Western than Indian, regardless of how many samosas their parents served at home.

The Practical Takeaway

The DAMM model is not yet a clinical tool. Its creators describe it as a framework designed to evolve as the science of host-microbe interactions deepens. But its implications are already actionable.

First, calorie labels underestimate the gap between high-fibre and low-fibre diets. If you are watching your weight and relying on packaged food counts, you are likely absorbing more than you think. Second, fibre is not merely roughage that passes through. It is the raw material that feeds the microbial community responsible for a meaningful share of your energy regulation. Third, traditional Indian staples — dal, sabzi, whole-grain roti, fermented foods like idli and dosa — are precisely the microbiome-enhancing foods that the DAMM study links to lower calorie absorption.

The irony is hard to miss. Millions of Indians left home seeking better opportunities and promptly abandoned the diet that their gut bacteria had spent millennia adapting to. The science now suggests that restoring even a portion of that diet could shift the calorie equation in ways that no gym membership can match.

For parents raising children in the US, UK or Canada, the message is pointed: the traditional thali is not nostalgia. It is a metabolic strategy that modern science is only beginning to understand.

Sources: PLOS ONE (Davis et al., 2026); npj Biofilms and Microbiomes (2025); Arizona State University Biodesign Institute
